items.title: Screenshots for the README and social preview image

labels.name: good first issue
labels.description: Good entry point for new contributors

items.body:
The README has a screenshot placeholder and the repo has no social preview image.

**Wanted**
- Screenshots of the homepage, the browse page with filters applied, and a project detail page (light and dark both welcome)
- A 1280x640 social preview image

Run `npm run dev` locally, capture, and add them under `docs/screenshots/`, then replace the `<!-- Screenshots go here -->` comment in the README.

items.title: Expand data/taxonomies/technologies.yaml

labels.name: good first issue
labels.description: Good entry point for new contributors

items.body:
The technology vocabulary is a starter set. Winners we cannot record cleanly today include hardware, non-English-ecosystem frameworks, and most AI tooling released in the last year.

**Task:** add canonical entries to `data/taxonomies/technologies.yaml`. Each needs a kebab-case `slug`, a display `name`, and a `type` from: language, framework, ai-model, ai-platform, database, cloud, hardware, blockchain, api, tool, platform, other.

Rules:
- One PR can add many technologies
- No duplicates or near-synonyms of an existing slug (check first)
- Only add things that actually appear in hackathon projects
- Run `npm run validate:data` before pushing

items.title: Add a Grid/List toggle to /projects

labels.name: good first issue
labels.description: Good entry point for new contributors

items.body:
The browse page renders cards only. A dense list view is better for scanning many results.

`WinnerRow` in `src/components/winner-card.tsx` is already written and unused — wire it up.

**Scope**
- A toggle in `src/components/results-toolbar.tsx` that sets `?view=list` / `?view=grid`
- `src/components/winner-browser.tsx` reads the param and picks the renderer
- Default stays grid; the param must survive filtering and pagination like every other param
- Add a Playwright assertion in `tests/e2e/smoke.spec.ts`

Keep it simple — no client state beyond the URL.

items.title: 🏆 Call for winners: MLH hackathons (2023–2026)

labels.name: good first issue
labels.description: Good entry point for new contributors

items.body:
We have no MLH events yet. Pick any MLH-affiliated hackathon, find its published winners, and submit them.

**How:** one [add-winner issue](../../issues/new?template=add-winner.yml) per project, or one PR per event via `npm run add:winner`.

**Needed per winner:** hackathon name + year, project name, award exactly as published, and a public source URL that confirms it (MLH results page, organizer announcement, Devpost gallery).

Comment which event you are taking so two people do not duplicate work.

items.title: 📌 Start here: how to add a hackathon winner

labels.name: good first issue
labels.description: Good entry point for new contributors

items.body:
Welcome! HackWinnerDB is an open database of projects that **won** hackathons. The main way to contribute is to submit a winner you know about.

## The only hard rule

**Every winner needs a public source URL that confirms the award.** A Devpost winner gallery, an organizer announcement, an official blog post, or a results page. No source, no entry.

## Three ways to contribute

**1. No code (2 minutes)** — open the [Add a hackathon winner form](../../issues/new?template=add-winner.yml). Give the hackathon, year, project, award, and source URL. A maintainer converts it to data.

**2. Pull request with help from the CLI**
```bash
npm install
npm run add:winner       # answers the prompts, writes the YAML for you
npm run validate:data
npm run check:duplicates
```
Then open a PR. One event per PR keeps review fast.

**3. Write the YAML by hand** — see [DATA_GUIDELINES.md](../blob/main/DATA_GUIDELINES.md).

## What we will not accept

- Winners with no public source
- Descriptions copied from Devpost, blogs, or README files — write your own two sentences
- Free-text technologies or categories; use the slugs in `data/taxonomies/`
- Participation with no award

Questions? Comment here.

items.title: Tell me what your ACP agent does when it wants to edit
items.body:
Not a code change — a report, and a genuinely useful one.

termesh shows an agent's edit as a reviewable diff when the agent checks with the client before
touching the file. Whether a given agent does that is a property of the agent, and often of its
configuration. `docs/support.md` has a table of what each one was measured doing; it currently
covers three.

If you use an ACP agent that is not on it, this answers the question in one command:

```bash
TERMESH_TEST_AGENT="<your agent argv>" TERMESH_TEST_EDIT=1 \
  cargo test -p termesh-agent --test live_agent -- --ignored --nocapture
```

It sends a real prompt, so it invokes a model and may cost you a few cents — a small or local
model is completely fine here, since the question is what the *agent* does with an edit, not how
good the edit is. It passes when the agent asks before editing and
the file is still untouched at that moment, and fails with what it found on disk when the agent
wrote first. **Both outcomes are useful** — please open an issue with the agent, its version, any
permission settings you had to change, and the output either way.

items.title: Language-server recipes for more languages
items.body:
`crates/lsp/src/recipe.rs` maps a detected project to the server command that serves it. Rust,
TypeScript/JavaScript, Python and Java have built-in recipes; everything else needs the user to
configure a command by hand.

A recipe is a few lines — the command, and `initializationOptions` if the server needs them (see
the existing entries at `recipe.rs:31` onward). Go (`gopls`), C/C++ (`clangd`), and Ruby
(`ruby-lsp`) are the obvious next ones.

What "done" looks like: the recipe, detection for that project type, a unit test that resolves it
with and without a workspace override, and a row in `docs/language-servers.md` saying how to
install the server. No server is bundled or downloaded — that is deliberate (ARCHITECTURE §12).

items.title: Add a tree-sitter grammar so more than Rust is highlighted
items.body:
Highlighting ships exactly one grammar. A TypeScript, Python or Java file gets full language
intelligence — diagnostics, go-to-definition, symbols, rename, formatting — but renders as plain
text, which surprises people who read "Tier 1 support" as covering both. `docs/support.md` is
explicit that the two advanced separately.

Adding one language is a small, self-contained change, and the same shape repeats for the next:

- add the crate to `[workspace.dependencies]` and `crates/syntax/Cargo.toml`
- add a variant to `Language` (`crates/syntax/src/lib.rs:24`)
- map the extension in `Language::from_path` (`:33`)
- add the `HighlightConfiguration` arm (`:80`), reusing the existing `CAPTURES` table

`CAPTURES` is deliberately short — a terminal has few colours to spend legibly — so fold the new
grammar's capture names onto the existing kinds rather than adding token classes. The Rust arm at
`:52` shows how aliases get folded.

Good candidates, roughly in order of demand: TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, Go, Java.

Please do one language per PR. Add a highlight test alongside the existing ones in that file, and
run `./scripts/verify.sh` — that is the whole gate.
